title: Who can afford to only squat and deadlift once a week?
summary: NH explains that he only squats and deadlifts heavy every 8 days because his technique is fully automated, while still training knee and hip patterns every two days with variations. He argues novices must practice these lifts several times a week to build skill, which should always stay ahead of strength. Bench is different: less technical but loses strength fast, so it needs higher frequency.

claims.claim: Almost all his lower body gains came from squat and deadlift variations; he never did hack squats, leg press, leg extensions or leg curls.
If you can do them properly, squats and deadlifts are your best friends for lower body hypertrophy, though he doesn't say they are enough for everyone.
He does heavy conventional deadlifts once every 8 days and heavy high-bar squats once every 8 days so he can recover from these taxing sessions.
He still trains a knee-flexion pattern and a hip hinge about every 2 days, using different variations, bars, lighter loads and more volume.
Chinese weightlifter Lu Xiaojun said he only did the Olympic lifts occasionally and focused on squats and deadlifts for strength, which matches NH's reasoning about mastered lifts.
Once neural adaptation to a lift is complete and form is automatic, you can lower the frequency of heavy work on it without problems.
Novices should squat and deadlift several times a week, recovery permitting, to ingrain form; not always heavy, using volume work, speed work, pause reps or deloads.
Videos and coaching cues help, but only repeated practice makes form stick for life; squatting and deadlifting once a week is not enough practice for a novice.
A novice's goal is to raise skill on every lift as high as possible; strength should rise but never exceed skill, or form breaks down.
He opposes powerlifting-style programs that add 5 lbs to the bar every session for novices, preferring focus on moving the bar perfectly.
Skill and technique decline much more slowly than strength and largely stay for life once built.
Strength is a transmission of energy; if technique is poor the transmission is not smooth, and a weaker person with better skill may outlift you.
High skill across many lifts gives a bodybuilder freedom to program; if he had to deadlift heavy every 4-5 days it would wreck his recovery, volume and ability to train daily.

numbers.frequency: every 4-5 days would be too much

claims.claim: Only people who have already accumulated enough skill can afford to squat and deadlift heavy just once a week; beginners should focus on skill and technique.
Bench press is much less technical than squat and deadlift, but it is the lift where he loses strength fastest, so he cannot bench only once a week.
